newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Pressure to raise S.Korea LNG demand expectations.
newsitem.headline: Pressure to raise S.Korea LNG demand expectations.

text.p: Demand for liquefied natural gas (LNG) in South Korea is rising with pressure for an upward revision of forecasts, government officials and economists said on Friday.

The country is in the process of switching increasingly to LNG at the expense of liquefied petroleum gas (LPG). At the same time a bottleneck on supply facilities is restricting some demand, the sources said.
These pressure are adding to a need to upgrade forecasts for Asia's second largest LNG buyer.
"South Korea's demand for LNG is exploding," said an economist at Korea Energy Economic Institute.
"Demand is even being controlled to some extent due to lack of LNG supply facilities. It's unlikely that the forecasts would be revised down."
LNG demand is seen rising to 18.2 million tonnes by 2000 from 12.1 million this year and 9.56 million last year, the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy said.
In a separate long-term forecast released in early 1996, the government projected demand in 2010 at 23.3 million tonnes.
A senior energy ministry official said the 1996 forecast was now outdated.
"When the ministry revises the forecasts at the end of this year, we are more likely to increase the figures," he said.
South Korea is Asia's second biggest LNG buyer behind Japan -- the world's biggest buyer.
Some analysts have said demand projections for Asia might be overstated, which could lead to a future supply glut.

Fereidun Fesharaki, a director of the energy think tank East-West Centre in Hawaii, told a gas conference in Singapore earlier this month that some supply projects might not be needed until after 2010 because of the overstated forecasts.
He singled out Yemen, Sakhalin, Papua New Guinea, Canada, Alaska and the Natuna and Wiriagar gas fields in Indonesia as projects that might find limited demand.
But in the case of South Korea, government officials and economists said they saw no reason to cut back expectations.
"We believe our forecast figures are quite accurate," said the energy ministry official.
South Korea is switching home fuel to LNG from LPG by 2000. Half the nation has already made the change.
LNG demand for heating and industrial use is growing sharply, the sources said.

"Demands are only seen rising under the circumstances. The only way we'd shrink our forecasts would be if the government sees a need to narrow foreign debt," said an official of state-run Korea Gas Corp (KOGAS).
It's forecasts are more bullish than that of the government.
KOGAS said LNG imports are expected to rise to 20.7 million tonnes in 2001 from 9.5 million tonnes last year. Import demand would hit 25 million tonnes in 2006 and 29.3 tonnes in 2010, it said.
KOGAS imports LNG from Indonesia, Malaysia, Brunei and Australia and is set to take deliveries from Gulf Arab Qatar in 1999 and Oman in the following year.

South Korea will finalise a deal with Qatar later this month to increase LNG supplies to 4.8 million tonnes a year for 25 years annually from the year 2000. Under its earlier deal, 2.4 million tonnes would initially be supplied in 1999.
Oman will provide 4.1 million tonnes of LNG annually for 25 years starting in early 2000.
South Korea currently has two long term agreements with Indonesia and one with Malaysia, and the rest are provided by short-term contracts.
--Seoul Newsroom (+822 727 5643)
